### EXT-103 — Published robot-evaluation counts range from tens of real trials to hundreds in simulation

**Finding.** In the checked primary papers, real-robot evaluation commonly
uses tens rather than hundreds of trials per policy–task condition: ALOHA uses
25 trials per real task/method; Octo reports 20 trials for a named
policy–task evaluation; OpenVLA uses 10 trials for each of 17 Bridge tasks,
10–12 in-distribution and 5–6 out-of-distribution rollouts per
Franka-tabletop policy–task condition, and 18/12 for one Franka-DROID
in-/out-of-distribution condition. Simulation counts are larger: ALOHA uses
50 trials per seed over three seeds, and OpenVLA’s LIBERO evaluation uses 500
trials per task suite per seed over three seeds. RT-2 reports more than 6,000
real robotic evaluation trials in aggregate, but that headline total is
distributed across models, tasks, and evaluation categories and is not a
per-cell count.

At a binary success probability near 0.5, the ordinary normal-approximation
95% half-width is approximately 19.6 percentage points at `n=25`, 13.9 at
`n=50`, 9.8 at `n=100`, 6.9 at `n=200`, and 4.9 at `n=400`. Thus, low tens of
real trials are established publication practice but provide coarse
condition-level success estimates; paper quality or evidential adequacy cannot
be inferred from the headline episode total alone.

**Status.** confirmed

**Evidence basis.** source-verified; derived

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with
  Low-Cost Hardware,” RSS 2023, Section V-C,
  <https://tonyzhaozh.github.io/aloha/aloha.pdf>, retrieved 2026-07-24.
  It reports one seed and 25 trials for real-world tasks, versus three seeds
  and 50 trials per seed for simulated tasks.
- Source: Octo Model Team et al., “Octo: An Open-Source Generalist Robot
  Policy,” RSS 2024, Appendix F.2,
  <https://octo-models.github.io/paper.pdf>, retrieved 2026-07-24. The CMU
  Baking evaluation reports 20 trials (four novel objects × five positions);
  the broader project page reports approximately 100 target demonstrations
  per task for finetuning.
- Source: Kim et al., “OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model,”
  CoRL 2024 / PMLR 270 (2025), Appendices B.1.1, B.3.1, and G.1,
  <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlresearch/v270/main/assets/kim25c/kim25c.pdf>,
  retrieved 2026-07-24. It reports 10 trials on each of 17 Bridge tasks,
  10–12/5–6 in-/out-of-distribution Franka-tabletop rollouts, 18/12
  Franka-DROID rollouts, and 500 LIBERO trials per task suite per seed over
  three seeds.
- Source: Zitkovich et al., “RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web
  Knowledge to Robotic Control,” CoRL 2023 / PMLR 229,
  <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v229/zitkovich23a.html>, retrieved
  2026-07-24. The abstract reports more than 6,000 robotic evaluation trials.
- Method: For binary success with `p=0.5`, computed the approximate 95%
  half-width as `1.96 * sqrt(0.25 / n)` for
  `n ∈ {25, 50, 100, 200, 400}`, then converted the results to percentage
  points. This is a descriptive precision calculation, not a prospective
  comparison-power analysis.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** This is a deliberately small set of
prominent examples, not a systematic distribution of robotics-paper episode
counts. Cells, tasks, seeds, initial conditions, and repeated trials are not
interchangeable independent units. The normal approximation is least reliable
near boundaries and at small `n`; exact or Wilson intervals should be used in
the actual analysis. Comparative studies require a design-specific power
analysis that accounts for pairing, clustering, multiplicity, and the smallest
effect of interest. “Published” is not equivalent to adequately powered.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `confirmed` at the checked source-specific scopes
  after verifying the per-cell counts in four primary papers and deriving the
  stated worst-case binary-success precision values.

### EXT-104 — Generalist public robot datasets contain tens of thousands to more than one million trajectories

**Finding.** Current prominent public generalist robot-learning releases are
orders of magnitude larger than a task-specific paper dataset. The current
BridgeData V2 project page reports 53,896 trajectories spanning 13 skills and
24 environments on a low-cost robot. DROID reports 76,000 demonstrations /
350 interaction hours spanning 564 scenes and 86 tasks, collected by 50
people across 13 institutions over 12 months. Open X-Embodiment aggregates
more than one million real-robot trajectories from 22 embodiments contributed
by more than 20 institutions. These scales describe broad generalist training
resources, not minimum sample sizes for a valuable or publishable specialized
dataset.

**Status.** confirmed

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: BridgeData V2 project page, “Dataset Composition,”
  <https://bridgedata-v2.github.io/>, retrieved 2026-07-24. The live page
  reports 53,896 trajectories, 13 skills, and 24 environments. Earlier paper
  versions report different trajectory totals, so the claim is explicitly
  scoped to the current project-page release.
- Source: DROID project-page overview,
  <https://droid-dataset.github.io/>, retrieved 2026-07-24. It reports 76,000
  trajectories / 350 hours, 564 scenes, 86 tasks, 50 collectors, and 12
  months; its hardware description states that collection was distributed
  across 13 institutions.
- Source: Open X-Embodiment project page,
  <https://robotics-transformer-x.github.io/>, and Google DeepMind release
  summary,
  <https://deepmind.google/blog/scaling-up-learning-across-many-different-robot-types/>,
  retrieved 2026-07-24. They report more than one million real-robot
  trajectories from 22 robot embodiments and a collaboration of more than 20
  institutions.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** Episode/trajectory definitions,
success filtering, task granularity, sensor schemas, and release versions
differ across datasets. Counts do not measure label quality, effective sample
size, distributional coverage, or fitness for a particular estimand. The
BridgeData paper and current project page expose version-dependent totals;
users must pin the exact release used. No inference is licensed that a new
specialized dataset must match these generalist scales.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `confirmed` at the cited release/date scopes after
  checking the three official project/release pages and preserving the
  BridgeData version-count qualification.

### EXT-105 — Current US funding routes depend on applicant type and project purpose

**Finding.** A roughly $55,000–$60,000 robot research station is better matched
to an equipment line within a broader academic research award, faculty startup
package, shared-lab budget, or small-business R&D project than to a standalone
NSF Major Research Instrumentation proposal. NSF states that MRI generally
supports requests from $100,000 to $4 million and is not accepting proposals
in the previously scheduled FY2026 window; it anticipates a new solicitation
and an October 15–November 16, 2026 submission window. For an eligible US
startup pursuing a commercializable robotics innovation, the NSF Seed Fund
currently lists robotics as a supported technology area, requires a Project
Pitch before an invited full proposal, and reports an average of $295,822
among active Phase I awards. NIH SBIR/STTR is a potential alternative only
when the project advances a health-related mission; NIH currently gives a
$323,090 Phase I budget guideline and states that new funding opportunities
are forthcoming following April 2026 program reauthorization.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited program/date scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: NSF, “Major Research Instrumentation Program,”
  <https://www.nsf.gov/od/oia/ia/major-research-instrumentation>, retrieved
  2026-07-24. The program page states the general $100,000–$4 million request
  range, the FY2026 pause, and the anticipated October 15–November 16, 2026
  window. Some institution-specific exceptions apply to the lower bound.
- Source: NSF Seed Fund, “How to Submit,”
  <https://seedfund.nsf.gov/how-to-submit/>, “Project Pitch,”
  <https://seedfund.nsf.gov/project-pitch/>, and “Robotics,”
  <https://seedfund.nsf.gov/topics/robotics/>, retrieved 2026-07-24. These
  pages document the Project Pitch gate and robotics topic.
- Source: NSF Seed Fund, “Recently Funded Phase I Companies,”
  <https://seedfund.nsf.gov/awardees/phase-1/>, retrieved 2026-07-24. The live
  page reports a $295,822 average award among active Phase I awards.
- Source: NIH SEED, “Understanding SBIR and STTR,”
  <https://seed.nih.gov/small-business-funding/small-business-program-basics/understanding-sbir-sttr>,
  and NIH SEED FAQ, <https://seed.nih.gov/faqs>, retrieved 2026-07-24. The
  program overview gives the $323,090 Phase I budget guideline; the FAQ
  records April 13, 2026 reauthorization and describes forthcoming notices.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** Program windows, solicitations,
budget caps, eligibility rules, and allowable-cost treatment can change.
An eligible applicant must verify the live solicitation and obtain its
institutional or company grants-office interpretation before submission.
The cited award averages are descriptive, not promised funding. A robot
purchase is not independently sufficient for an award: the proposal must
justify a qualifying research or commercialization project, milestones,
personnel, and the equipment's necessity. Academic startup funds, ordinary
research-grant equipment lines, shared facilities, industry sponsorship,
vendor loans, and paid pilots are common practical routes but were not
exhaustively quantified here.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `confirmed at the cited program/date scope` after
  checking current official NSF and NIH program pages.

recovered simulator bars' 60-label lattice. In a declared aggregate
Beta-binomial sensitivity that samples both ten-trial real cells and simulator
cells while discounting simulator evidence to 10, 30, or 60 binary-label
equivalents, the probability that the sampled simulator winner is also the
sampled real winner is .20728–.21964 across Beta(.5,.5), Beta(1,1), and
Beta(2,2) priors. Expected sampled-real regret is 8.358–9.649 percentage
points. The exact displayed simulator winner remains simulator-best with
probability .28960–.43773, so the particular displayed pair is unstable while
the broader decision mismatch persists under this aggregate model.

### EXT-125 — Unaffiliated researchers have private funding routes but cannot receive ordinary NSF awards directly

**Finding.** Under NSF's current PAPPG, an unaffiliated individual cannot
receive direct NSF funding. An eligible US small business is a different
applicant type: for NSF SBIR/STTR, it must satisfy ownership and size rules,
and the principal investigator must be employed more than 50% by the company
during the award. Current private alternatives explicitly accessible without
an academic affiliation include: Manifund, where anyone may publish a
proposal and science/technology and technical AI safety are named cause
areas; Emergent Ventures, which accepts applications from thinkers and doers
worldwide; and Experiment, which encourages independent science but currently
reports a small $3,381 average funded-project size. Larger fellowship-style
routes exist but impose program fit: Astera offers 12–18-month fully funded
open-public-goods residencies with $125,000–$250,000 annual salary and a
negotiated project budget; Astera explicitly supports projects before their
eventual nonprofit/for-profit form is known and allows commercial-interest
terms to be negotiated during application. Activate offers more than $300,000
over two years, takes no equity, and is specifically designed for scientists
launching hard-technology companies. Manifund's route is instead bounded by
501(c)(3) public-benefit requirements and a grant agreement, so its funds
cannot be assumed to be unrestricted startup capital. A current public
Manifund grant agreement requires substantive project changes to receive
prior written approval and requires unspent money to be returned at the end
of the grant period.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited program/date scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: NSF, current PAPPG landing page and Chapter I.E.3,
  <https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg> and
  <https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-1-pre-submission>, retrieved
  2026-07-24. The current page identifies NSF 24-1 plus 2025–2026 supplements;
  Chapter I states that unaffiliated individuals are ineligible for direct
  funding.
- Source: NSF Seed Fund, “SBIR/STTR Eligibility and Requirements,”
  <https://seedfund.nsf.gov/solicitation-eligibility/>, retrieved 2026-07-24.
  It states the under-500-employee and US-ownership tests and the requirement
  that the PI be more than 50% employed by the business during the project.
  It also states that registrations are unnecessary for a Project Pitch but
  that the company needs active SAM, Research.gov, and SBA Company Registry
  registrations to submit a full proposal.
- Source: Manifund, “Funding Your Project,”
  <https://manifund.org/about/open-call>, retrieved 2026-07-24. It states that
  anyone can create a public proposal and lists science and technology and
  technical AI safety among its usual cause areas; it also conditions funding
  on 501(c)(3)-compatible public benefit and a signed grant agreement.
- Source: Manifund, public recipient grant agreement for “Seiche,” Sections
  2.2–2.3,
  <https://manifund.org/projects/seiche-a-tamper-evident-early-warning-system-for-dollar-funding-stress/agreement>,
  retrieved 2026-07-24. It requires prior written agreement for substantive
  project changes and return of any unspent balance at the end of the grant
  period. Recipient-specific agreements may differ, so the signed agreement
  remains controlling.
- Source: Mercatus Center, “Emergent Ventures,”
  <https://www.mercatus.org/emergent-ventures>, retrieved 2026-07-24. It
  describes a low-overhead fellowship and grant program for scalable,
  socially beneficial ideas and states that grants are awarded worldwide.
- Source: Experiment, “Start an Experiment,”
  <https://experiment.com/start>, retrieved 2026-07-24. It encourages
  independent science, uses all-or-nothing crowdfunding, and reports 1,415
  funded projects, a 47.97% success rate, and a $3,381 average project size.
- Source: Astera, “Residency,” <https://astera.org/residency/>, retrieved
  2026-07-24. It describes a 12–18-month open-public-goods residency, the
  salary range, negotiated project-expense support, and approximately
  twice-yearly application cycles. It explicitly states that supported work
  may later become a nonprofit, for-profit company, or public-domain output
  and that commercial-interest terms can be negotiated during application.
- Source: Activate, “The Activate Fellowship,”
  <https://activate.org/the-fellowship>, retrieved 2026-07-24. It describes
  a two-year US hard-technology startup fellowship providing more than
  $300,000 and taking no equity.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** Private programs are competitive,
may alter their terms or application windows, and may reject a project on
mission fit. Published maximums or averages are not award promises.
Crowdfunding requires audience-building and is not a credible standalone plan
for a $55,000 robot at the reported average project size. Private payments
may have tax, contracting, intellectual-property, residency, or
fiscal-sponsorship consequences that require applicant-specific professional
advice. Creating a company changes eligibility but does not make a research
project fundable by itself; SBIR requires a qualifying commercialization
project and full compliance with the solicitation. Neither grant-funded
equipment nor grant-produced intellectual property should be transferred into
a later company unless the agreement expressly permits it or the funder gives
written approval.

**Status history.**

### EXT-121 — OSCAR releases paired videos but not the outcome table behind its printed rates

**Finding.** At immutable Hugging Face dataset revision
`db5edfaef285c15d0a41d5115177a983c08b4f5f`, the OSCAR policy-rollout release
contains 441 paired real/OSCAR overlay videos: exactly 63 session IDs for each
of seven policies and 1,383,864,176 video bytes. The dataset viewer exposes
only a video column; no canonical real-success or GPT-5 judgment table is
released in that dataset. However, every release session ID joins to
RoboArena `DataDump_08-05-2025` at revision
`036d031087b892bd15d99d1d6406eedba4c902f7`: all 63 joined records have a
task instruction, the exact seven-policy roster, and 441 valid real
binary-success outcomes. Those real outcomes select pi0-FAST; the printed
world-model bars select PG-FAST+, giving 3.1746 percentage points of joined
release-real regret. This cross-vector diagnostic is not an exact
matched-session evaluator estimate because every printed OSCAR world-model
rate lies on a 65-session lattice and the historical printed real bars use
another aggregation. The 63-session release therefore still does not
reproduce or reconcile the printed evaluator rates. This establishes a
release boundary, not that the original 65-session analysis is wrong.

**Status.** confirmed

**Evidence basis.** source-verified; reproduced inventory and join

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: OSCAR official project
  <https://wuzy2115.github.io/oscar-project-page/>, repository
  <https://github.com/wuzy2115/oscar-public>, and dataset
  <https://huggingface.co/datasets/zywu2115/OSCAR_policy_rollout>, retrieved
  2026-07-24.
- Method:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-study-design/audit_oscar_rollout_release.py`
  resolves the dataset revision, pages the immutable Hugging Face tree, parses
  policy/session IDs, sums bytes, and compares denominators.
- Join method:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-study-design/audit_oscar_roboarena_join.py`
  resolves both immutable dataset revisions, joins all release session paths
  to RoboArena metadata, verifies instruction/roster/outcome coverage, and
  writes only aggregate policy totals. It does not write session IDs,
  instructions, evaluator identities, feedback, or row-level outcomes.
- Reproduction: run
  `.venv/bin/python research/prospective-study-design/audit_oscar_rollout_release.py --retrieved 2026-07-24 --out research/prospective-study-design/result-oscar-rollout-release.json`.
  Expected results include 1,388 tree entries, 441 paired videos, seven
  policies × 63 sessions, and
  `denominator_matches_printed_rate_lattice=false`.
- Join reproduction: run
  `.venv/bin/python research/prospective-study-design/audit_oscar_roboarena_join.py --oscar-revision db5edfaef285c15d0a41d5115177a983c08b4f5f --roboarena-repo RoboArena/DataDump_08-05-2025 --roboarena-revision 036d031087b892bd15d99d1d6406eedba4c902f7 --retrieved 2026-07-24 --out research/prospective-study-design/result-oscar-roboarena-join.json`,
  then `.venv/bin/python
  research/prospective-study-design/analyze_oscar_joined_panel.py`. Expected

  rosters in 63/63 sessions, and 441/441 valid real binary outcomes. Expected
  diagnostic results are joined real winner pi0-FAST, printed world-model
  winner PG-FAST+, 3.174603 pp joined real regret, and Pearson
  `r=0.748490`; artifact:
  `research/prospective-study-design/result-oscar-joined-panel.json`.

  reproduced against RoboArena `DataDump_07-17-2026` revision

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** The join does not identify why 63
rather than 65 sessions were released, whether sessions were removed, or which

### EXT-123 — Generic policy-selection uncertainty and regret are not novel contributions here

**Finding.** A bounded 2026-07-24 primary-source collision search found that
the generic methodological ingredients of this audit's decision analyses are
already occupied. Yang et al. (AISTATS 2022) formally treat offline policy
selection using posterior belief distributions and arbitrary downstream
selection metrics. WHALE defines `Regret@k` as the real-value loss between the
best policy overall and the best policy in the evaluator's top-k set.
Nakamura et al. (CoRL 2025) use regret to identify prediction errors that
degrade downstream robot performance. Recent robot-world-model work directly
evaluates ranking/MMRV and matched policy-evaluator behavior: SC3-Eval reports
Pearson/MMRV over seven real VLA checkpoints, RoboWorld reports Pearson .989
and Spearman .970 over eight policies, and GigaWorld-1/WMBench reports seven
world models, four action encodings, and more than 324,000 simulated policy
rollouts paired with real executions. A standalone contribution therefore
cannot simply be “use regret/top-k/posteriors instead of correlation” or
“benchmark world models for policy evaluation.”

A 2026-07-25 primary-source expansion further found close collisions in
sequential robot-policy comparison, active robot experiment selection,
off-environment evaluation using imperfect simulation plus offline real data,
high-confidence off-policy evaluation and safe policy improvement,
interaction-budget policy selection, and selective-prediction risk/coverage.
The exact prospectively frozen robot-evaluator study remains only a
low-confidence candidate gap. It is not justified to claim moderate
distinctness or choose sample size from candidate count alone; a held-out
study needs a prespecified independent unit, target environment population,
loss, decision rule, outcome custody, and acceptance-criterion-based
precision or power calculation.

**Status.** confirmed

**Evidence basis.** source-verified at bounded-search scope

**Evidence and trace.**

- Yang et al., “Offline Policy Selection under Uncertainty,” AISTATS 2022,
  PMLR 151:4376–4396,
  <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v151/yang22a.html>.
- Zhang et al., “WHALE,” arXiv:2411.05619v1, Appendix B.4, Equation 9,
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05619>.
- Nakamura et al., “Not All Errors Are Made Equal,” CoRL 2025, PMLR
  270:4051–4065,
  <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v270/nakamura25a.html>.
- Tseng et al., “SC3-Eval,” arXiv:2606.18610v3,
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18610>; Jeon et al., “RoboWorld,”
  arXiv:2607.01060v4, <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01060>; GigaWorld Team,
  “GigaWorld-1,” arXiv:2607.02642,
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02642>.
- Katdare, Jiang, and Driggs-Campbell, “Marginalized Importance Sampling for
  Off-Environment Policy Evaluation,” CoRL 2023,
  <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v229/katdare23a.html>; Thomas, Theocharous,
  and Ghavamzadeh, high-confidence off-policy evaluation and improvement,
  AAAI/ICML 2015,
  <https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/9541> and
  <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v37/thomas15.html>; Bozkurt et al.,
  “Adaptive Policy Selection and Fine-Tuning under Online Interaction
  Budgets,” L4DC 2026,
  <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v331/bozkurt26a.html>.
- Selective-prediction primary sources:
  <https://jmlr.org/papers/v24/21-0048.html> and
  <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v26/24-0452.html>.
- Search trace:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-study-design/review-literature-collision.md`.
- Expanded audit and independent challenge:
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/primary-source-audit.md`
  and
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/review-source-audit.md`.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** This is a collision search, not a
systematic review. Full-text method comparison remains required before

### EXT-124 — The released OSCAR session count has little power for modest post-selection regret

**Finding.** Under a prospective seven-policy paired-session simulation with a
5-percentage-point non-negligible regret margin, familywise coverage of all 42
ordered policy comparisons, and 4,000 fixed-seed replicates per cell, 63
sessions flag the entire sampled evaluator top-tied set in only .6–.7% of
7.5-point mismatch scenarios, 1.1–1.2% of 10-point mismatch scenarios, and
34.4–47.9% of 27.5-point mismatch scenarios. At 126 sessions the large-effect
rate is 74.9–87.4%, and at 252 it is 98.4–99.8%. Positive-control false flags
are at most .2% in the declared cells. Labeling all 63 sessions can therefore
describe that finite release, but this model and rule do not support a
well-powered future-session claim for modest regret above a 5-point margin.

**Status.** confirmed

**Evidence basis.** derived; reproduced; model-conditional

**Evidence and trace.**

- External design anchor: the 63 shared sessions × seven policies in EXT-121.
- Method:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-study-design/simulate_oscar_labeling_power.py`
  uses seed 20260724 and 4,000 replicates per cell. Real/evaluator binary
  outcomes share a Gaussian session-difficulty random intercept with sigma 0
  or 1.25; calibrated logistic-normal intercepts preserve declared marginals.
  The one-sided paired rule uses Bonferroni familywise alpha .05 over 42
  ordered pairs and flags only if every evaluator top-tied policy is shown more
  than 5 points worse than a real competitor.
- Reproduction: run
  `.venv/bin/python research/prospective-study-design/simulate_oscar_labeling_power.py`
  and
  `.venv/bin/python -m pytest research/prospective-study-design/test_simulate_oscar_labeling_power.py -q`.
  Expected artifact:
  `research/prospective-study-design/result-oscar-labeling-power.json`.
- Interpretation:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-study-design/protocol-oscar-labeling-pilot.md`.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** Scenario rates and dependence are
not fitted to OSCAR. Prespecifying a comparator, sample splitting, or changing
the operational margin changes power. Monte Carlo standard error is at most
.79 percentage points. The calculation does not turn the released convenience
sessions into a sampled future-session population.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `confirmed` as a reproducible,
  model-conditional design result after the scenario grid and tests completed.

### EXT-129 — Every released OSCAR paired video fully decodes under one media geometry

**Finding.** At OSCAR dataset revision
`db5edfaef285c15d0a41d5115177a983c08b4f5f`, all 441 released paired videos
downloaded and fully decoded without error. The files are 441 distinct SHA-256
objects totaling 1,383,864,176 bytes. Every file has one H.264/yuv420p video
stream, no audio stream, 1280×480 geometry, and 10 fps; durations range from
2.5 to 40.0 seconds with a 34.2-second median. A seven-policy visual sample
confirmed the release convention: the left half is the generated rollout with
a visible skeleton overlay and the right half is the real rollout. The uniform
geometry makes a generated-half labeling packet technically executable, but
the overlay prevents source blinding. A deterministic,
outcome-independent selection of 10 sessions × seven policies was then
converted into a 70-clip blinded-policy base packet. All crops succeeded, and
every decoded output-frame checksum matched its corresponding 640×480 source
crop. The two independently ordered rater sheets omit policy and session
identities; the unblinding map is stored separately.

**Status.** confirmed

**Evidence basis.** source-verified; reproduced media audit

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: OSCAR policy-rollout dataset
  <https://huggingface.co/datasets/zywu2115/OSCAR_policy_rollout>, immutable
  revision `db5edfaef285c15d0a41d5115177a983c08b4f5f`, retrieved 2026-07-24.
- Method:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-study-design/audit_oscar_video_integrity.py`

  selects the ten sessions with the smallest SHA-256 of

  Expected aggregate output: 70/70 clips, zero crop failures, zero frame

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** Decode integrity does not establish

### EXT-131 — OSCAR's released open-loop replay cannot by itself establish screening utility

**Finding.** OSCAR's published policy-evaluation procedure initializes from a
recorded first frame and conditions on the robot action sequence recorded
during the corresponding real execution. That procedure can be applied to new
sessions to test whether the evaluator's judgment tracks future real
preferences or outcomes (E2). It cannot, without a separate closed-loop or
otherwise pre-execution action generator, establish that OSCAR selects which
policies to test before spending those real robot trials (E7). Treating the
recorded actions as a cost-free screening input would count the physical
execution that produced them as if it had not occurred.

**Status.** confirmed

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, derived

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Wu and Gao, “OSCAR: Omni-Embodiment Action-Conditioned World Model
  for Robotics,” arXiv:2606.04463v2, Section 5.4, especially the statement
  that each episode is autoregressively rolled out “from the recorded first
  frame and the given robot action,” and Appendix A.10.4's pairing of every
  generated rollout with its corresponding real-robot video,
  <https://arxiv.org/html/2606.04463v2>, retrieved 2026-07-24.
- Source: official OSCAR inference repository
  <https://github.com/wuzy2115/oscar-public>, commit
  `4dea2f657e221b0ff24c895fcc8ab4d46d5a9adb`, retrieved 2026-07-24.
  The public inference interface accepts a first frame, skeleton video, and
  prompt. Its DROID demo converts already-normalized joint states plus camera
  intrinsics/extrinsics into that skeleton video.
- Method: Trace the temporal provenance of every evaluator input. A screening
  policy must be chosen before the physical outcome-generating execution.
  Here the conditioning action sequence is a descendant of that execution,
  so the released open-loop procedure fails the pre-execution condition.
- Local protocol:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-study-design/protocol-e2-e7-prospective-study.md`
  freezes the non-circularity gate and a conditional randomized E7 design for
  a future closed-loop evaluator.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** A private OSCAR closed-loop system
may exist, and a new public implementation could satisfy the gate. This
finding does not claim that OSCAR cannot be extended to closed loop; it applies
to the published/released open-loop policy-evaluation procedure.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `confirmed` for the released open-loop procedure
  after the paper, inference interface, and action provenance were checked.

### EXT-134 — OSCAR's normalized-state skeleton renderer is CPU-executable, but the raw-data bridge and model inference are not thereby validated

**Finding.** At OSCAR public-code commit
`4dea2f657e221b0ff24c895fcc8ab4d46d5a9adb`, the bundled DROID demo converts
normalized joint angles, gripper openness, camera intrinsics, and
camera-to-base extrinsics into a skeleton overlay without a GPU. The declared
demo requirements are not sufficient at that commit: the renderer explicitly
requests ImageIO's `pyav` writer, but `demo/requirements.txt` declares
`imageio[ffmpeg]` and not PyAV. The unmodified renderer completed all 90
bundled frames after `av==15.1.0` was added to a disposable environment; both
outputs fully decoded as H.264, 1280×720, 15-fps videos.

This execution validates the normalized-array-to-overlay plumbing on the
bundled sample only. It does not establish that raw RoboArena records can
recover valid camera matrices, nor that OSCAR-2B generation succeeds. The
public repository separately recommends Linux x86_64, CUDA 12.4 or newer, and
at least 24 GB of GPU memory for inference.

**Status.** confirmed at the pinned public-code/sample scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, reproduced

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: official OSCAR inference repository,

### EXT-137 — The public artifacts do not yet define an inference-valid RoboArena-to-OSCAR evaluator

**Finding.** At the pinned public revisions, the released RoboArena robot-state
fields can be mapped to OSCAR's Franka/Robotiq skeleton representation with
near-machine-precision kinematic agreement, but two inference-critical
transformations remain unidentified.

First, all 115 post-OSCAR fixed-policy records have finite, dimensionally
stable state arrays, but 114 contain 400 states and one contains 132, with no
timestamps. A decoded-frame census of all 115 matched left-camera videos found
401 frames for every 400-state record and 132 frames for the 132-state record;
all videos are H.264, 512×288, and 10 fps. The state/video offset therefore
cannot be inferred from array lengths alone.

Second, OSCAR's public inference path documents 81-frame, 480-by-640 outputs
and exposes a start-frame plus fixed-frame-count interface. A decoded-frame
census of the immutable 441-video release found 132 distinct lengths spanning
25–400 frames; only six videos have exactly 81 frames. The repository
mentions a `pick_best_eval_start()` helper in an unreleased/private or oracle
context, but does not publish the policy-evaluation rule for selecting,
downsampling, padding, extending, stitching, or aggregating long trajectories.
A successful 81-frame generation would consequently establish execution of
the public short-interface path, not reproduction of the paper's policy
evaluator.

Across all 45,732 states, OSCAR's `panda_robotiq.urdf` with
`robotiq_arg2f_base_link` as the end effector reproduces the released
Cartesian translation to at most \(4.2341\times10^{-8}\) m and rotation to at
most \(8.5797\times10^{-8}\) rad when the last three Cartesian coordinates
are interpreted as extrinsic xyz Euler angles in radians. The axis-angle
alternative has median 0.3335-rad and maximum 2.5907-rad rotational error.
This closes the released joint-state dimensions, units, orientation
convention, end-effector mapping, and URDF consistency without GPU compute.

The remaining camera bridge is also not turnkey. OSCAR reports estimating
intrinsics with MoGe-v2 and camera-to-base pose with CtRNet-X, followed by
manual overlay inspection. At pinned CtRNet-X code, the DROID entry point
reads intrinsics from ZED SVO data, while the checked RoboArena release
contains MP4 and NPZ artifacts but no SVO. CtRNet-X's declared
Python 3.8/Torch 1.10/CUDA 11.3 stack is not the same environment as OSCAR's
CUDA-12.4-or-newer inference stack. The official downloadable CtRNet-X CLIP
archive also does not contain the exact paths hard-coded by the DROID script.
Separate immutable environments plus a recorded adapter and quantitative
known-calibration oracles are required before an unlabelled RoboArena overlay
can count as validated calibration.

The public source also fixes a conditional gripper-sign conversion, but not
its applicability to the released RoboArena export. At DROID platform commit
`33ae6a67274f36d2e29525b86f23a56616ef43a7`, `gripper_position` is
`1 - width/max_width`, so zero is open and one closed. The pinned OSCAR
renderer calls its value `gripper_openness` and increases rendered finger
separation with the value. Direct DROID-runtime input therefore maps as
`openness = 1 - gripper_position`. The exact RoboArena exporter or
timestamp-aligned known-open/known-closed release records are still required
before applying that conversion to the released NPZ field.

**Status.** confirmed at the pinned public-artifact scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, reproduced

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: OSCAR paper, arXiv:2606.04463v2, Appendix A.10.1–A.10.3,
  <https://arxiv.org/html/2606.04463v2>, and official inference repository
  <https://github.com/wuzy2115/oscar-public>, commit
  `4dea2f657e221b0ff24c895fcc8ab4d46d5a9adb`, retrieved 2026-07-24.
- Source: MoGe official repository <https://github.com/microsoft/MoGe>,
  commit `925b8ed835a7a9cdb7578ba15c658a0afc969030`; resolved
  `Ruicheng/moge-2-vitl-normal` revision
  `b135031bae30b5ac2ae141a0e68717795ce38340`, model LFS SHA-256
  `280741fd09bc3f403ccff9967784c2a391b52d2c0742ae3efdb21d9f90cc1a01`.
- Source: CtRNet-X official repository
  <https://github.com/darthandvader/CtRNet-X>, commit
  `e95562f6a753059865ad679fe57fe5e32384c99c`, and paper
  <https://arxiv.org/html/2409.10441>, retrieved 2026-07-24. The official
  Google Drive archives were downloaded without executing their models:
  CLIP archive SHA-256
  `940301f05b2bef239937f8ea30b211de0d0de14793aaecd3dde29d1dc6701751`
  and pose archive SHA-256
  `18ab54f54794973fff51fc68844f43fa19bac488bbb304bcf485af8ec8ba6ff4`.
- Source: RoboArena `DataDump_07-17-2026`, revision
  `7931db81f3f6a48a3245427f7213a4c461f92ccc`.
- Reproduction:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/oscar-input-reconstruction/audit_historical_input_contract.py`
  writes `result-historical-input-contract.json`; it uses a restricted
  NumPy-only unpickler and does not access outcomes or retain identifiers.
  `audit_historical_state_kinematics.py` writes
  `result-historical-state-kinematics.json` from all 45,732 states.
  `audit_outcome_blind_input_validity.py` writes
  `result-outcome-blind-input-validity.json`; it fixes the 441-video input to
  upstream artifact SHA-256
  `8028633b7c789a87c17ff1adaad42c12778b63b5a5a090add60e9bd54a21c2b0`,
  source revision `db5edfaef285c15d0a41d5115177a983c08b4f5f`, and
  path/file-hash manifest root
  `6f59686840f85b047f5fcb899bd164d643f43882987d27c9f9522f37ecd9037e`.
  Canonical result SHA-256 values are
  `47457fe824483365dc9d5c45bc76a41ba58eb493fea411f054f3e1ad21c8f63e`
  for the 115-video historical census and
  `99d0e617be7f8fc0ab43ef8dec71b892859551d4a12f3f1c59296d1f707caa14`
  for the combined input-validity audit. Independent read-only re-review
  reproduced both byte-for-byte after 33 focused tests passed.
  `audit_gpu_pre_spend_math.py` writes
  `result-gpu-pre-spend-math.json` and has adjacent known-answer tests for the
  normal-approximation diagnostics and exact binomial bounds.
  `review-pre-spend-audit.md` records the source/code inspection, model and
  archive pins, validation matrix, statistical review, and staged stop rules.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** A private or not-yet-released
OSCAR/RoboArena conversion pipeline may specify the missing temporal and
calibration conventions. Author-supplied details could resolve rather than
invalidate these gaps. Until then, neither a visually plausible overlay nor a
successful 81-frame generation identifies the target policy evaluator.
Calibration must recover withheld known intrinsics/extrinsics within frozen
error thresholds, the state/video offset must be selected on development
episodes and confirmed on a session-level holdout, and the long-trajectory
conversion and score aggregation must be fixed without outcomes. The
independent human control gate and the exact A/B statistical estimator remain
separate prerequisites to scientific inference.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `confirmed at the pinned public-artifact scope`

### EXT-138 — Current Runpod pod prices make a bounded smoke inexpensive but do not bound the full experiment

**Finding.** Runpod's official GPU pricing page, marked updated
2026-07-17, lists on-demand pod rates for 48 GB GPUs of $0.44/hour for A40,
$0.53/hour for RTX A6000, $0.84/hour for RTX 6000 Ada, and $0.99/hour for
L40S. The same page separately prices storage, including container and
running-volume disk at $0.10/GB/month. These are posted rates, not availability
or a performance guarantee.

The former 1.9-GPU-hour estimate is only the arithmetic extrapolation
\(115\times1\) minute from OSCAR's reported approximately one minute per
documented 81-frame output on its tested Blackwell GPU. It excludes
environment construction, calibration models, retries, repeated seeds,
storage, and the unresolved conversion of 25–400-frame policy rollouts. It
therefore cannot serve as a full-project cost estimate. A first execution
smoke can be bounded independently by a three-GPU-hour or $3 compute stop.

The subsequent layerwise-diagnostic setup and launch sequence obtained one
secure-cloud A40 at the quoted $0.44/hour rate using image
`runpod/pytorch:1.0.2-cu1281-torch280-ubuntu2404`, whose provider-reported
digest was
`sha256:0a360022e8de4375af99430f84e8b38951acc397252163a37ceac7204d01be35`.
The scientific attempt itself stopped before model loading after 25 seconds
at most, an arithmetic compute estimate of $0.0030556 rather than an invoice.
Through attempt 07, five observed runtimes totaled at least 2,630 GPU-seconds,
or $0.3214 at the quoted rate. That historical lower bound excludes the later
attempt-08 build, canary, readiness, and science Pods and must not be presented
as current cumulative spend.

Attempt-08 science-v3 used the same image digest and A40 rate. Its provider

### EXT-127 — Paid independent pre-submission review exists but is not journal peer review

**Finding.** Researchers can hire experts for scientific critique,
statistical checking, reproducibility audit, and pre-submission manuscript
review. Current commercial services and freelance marketplaces explicitly
offer those functions. This author-commissioned work does not replace the
independent peer review managed by a journal or conference. Reviewers should
be selected for relevant expertise and conflicts, confidentiality, payment,
scope, and any later scholarly contribution should be handled transparently.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited service/date scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: AJE, “Pre-submission Peer Review,”
  <https://www.aje.com/services/pre-submission-peer-review>, retrieved
  2026-07-24. The service explicitly states that it provides expert feedback
  before submission and does not replace formal journal peer review.
- Source: Kolabtree, marketplace and service overview,
  <https://www.kolabtree.com/> and
  <https://www.kolabtree.com/how-it-works>, retrieved 2026-07-24. The current
  pages offer scientific consulting, statistical review, manuscript review,
  and contracting with individual experts under a defined statement of work.
- Source: Committee on Publication Ethics, “Ethical Guidelines for Peer
  Reviewers,” <https://doi.org/10.24318/2019.1.4>, retrieved 2026-07-24.
  The guidance requires objective critique, confidentiality, and declaration
  of relevant conflicts for formal scholarly peer review.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** Marketplace membership, credentials,
hourly rates, and service labels do not establish review quality or
independence. Prices vary with field, scope, seniority, turnaround, code/data
access, and whether recomputation is required. Venue-specific authorship,
acknowledgment, conflict, and third-party confidentiality policies must be
checked before sharing an unpublished manuscript.

**Status history.**

### EXT-139 — The broad weak-evaluator exploitation question is occupied

**Finding.** Existing empirical work already demonstrates several versions of
the broad claim that optimizing against an imperfect or weaker evaluator can
increase the proxy score without commensurate improvement, and sometimes with
deterioration, on a stronger or separately defined target.

Gao, Schulman, and Hilton use a synthetic gold reward model and a learned proxy
reward model to measure reward-model overoptimization under both reinforcement
learning and best-of-\(n\) sampling. Burns et al. directly study stronger
students trained from weaker-model supervision; stronger students often exceed
their supervisors, but naive weak supervision does not recover the strong
model's full capability and the reported method does not succeed on their
ChatGPT preference-data setting. More recent preprints give more direct
collisions: Zhou reports self-play increasing a reference-free judge's pass
rate while exact-match accuracy remains flat, and Helff et al. report
RLVR-trained models exploiting an extensional verifier in a way detected by an
isomorphic verifier.

These sources make “can a stronger model game a weak evaluator?” an occupied
question rather than a sufficient new contribution. A bounded open-model
experiment is technically executable, but a credible new project needs a
narrower estimand or intervention, such as prespecified model-selection regret,
safety-threshold error, a target-aligned scarce-reference design, or a
prospective mitigation that is confirmed on an untouched task or model family.
None of these studies identifies a general law for future superhuman systems.

**Status.** provisional at the bounded 2022–2026 primary-source search scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, not independently reproduced

**Evidence and trace.**

- Gao, Schulman, and Hilton, “Scaling Laws for Reward Model
  Overoptimization,” <https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760>, retrieved
  2026-07-24.
- Burns et al., “Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities
  With Weak Supervision,” official project summary and paper,
  <https://openai.com/index/weak-to-strong-generalization/> and
  <https://cdn.openai.com/papers/weak-to-strong-generalization.pdf>, retrieved
  2026-07-24.
- Zhou, “More Convincing, Not More Correct: Self-Play Reward Hacking of
  Reference-Free LLM Judges,” <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05904>, retrieved
  2026-07-24.
- Helff et al., “LLMs Gaming Verifiers: RLVR can Lead to Reward Hacking,”
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15149>, retrieved 2026-07-24.
- Anthropic Alignment Science, “Recommendations for Technical AI Safety
  Research Directions,”
  <https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/recommended-directions/>, retrieved
  2026-07-24. Its scalable-oversight section recommends empirical testbeds
  that distinguish an accessible systematically erroneous proxy \(R\) from
  target \(R^*\).

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** This was a focused collision check,
not a systematic review. The two 2026 sources are recent preprints and have
not been independently reproduced here. Their task, model, and evaluator
settings do not establish transport to open-ended human-preference oversight
or future superhuman models. Before claiming novelty, a project must complete
a broader literature review and reproduce at least one baseline in the exact
planned stack.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `provisional at the bounded 2022–2026
  primary-source search scope` after checking direct empirical work on reward
  overoptimization, weak supervision, self-play judge gaming, and verifier
  shortcuts.

### EXT-142 — AuditBench is an executable substrate, not a decision-validity result

**Finding.** Anthropic's AuditBench release makes controlled studies of
hidden behavior and alignment auditing technically executable without first
constructing every model organism from scratch. The official release reports
56 language models spanning 14 implanted hidden behaviors and four training
configurations, based primarily on Llama 3.3 70B Instruct with replication on
Qwen3-32B. The public repository includes training-data generation,
SFT/DPO/KTO fine-tuning, inference, 21 auditing-agent affordances, scoring, and
visualization code; its Hugging Face organization publishes model and dataset
artifacts.

The release does not itself answer whether evaluator gaming changes a
prespecified model-selection or safety decision, or whether a probability
sample of target-aligned audits prevents that decision error. Its reported
endpoint is whether an auditor identifies the implanted hidden objective.
Using it for the proposed decision study therefore requires adding candidate
decisions, a separately measurable intended target, audit inclusion
probabilities, and decision-error or regret estimands.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited 2026 release scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Anthropic Alignment Science, “AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment
  Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors,” 2026-03-10,
  <https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/auditbench/>, sections “Model
  organisms,” “Results,” and release links, retrieved 2026-07-24.
- Source: `safety-research/auditing-agents`, public AuditBench repository,
  <https://github.com/safety-research/auditing-agents>, README sections
  “Setup,” “Running Experiments,” and “Creating Model Organisms,” main branch
  as displayed 2026-07-24. The README recommends H100-class GPUs for 70B
  models, exposes an optional LoRA-training environment, and documents a
  canonical all-techniques run with 16 independent runs and up to 200,000
  tokens per run.
- Source: Anthropic AuditBench Hugging Face organization,
  <https://huggingface.co/auditing-agents>, model, dataset, and collection

- Method: Checked the official release's model-organism and evaluation scope,
  then checked the linked repository for runnable components, hardware
  assumptions, run budgets, and training support, and the linked Hugging Face
  organization for artifact availability.
- Access limitations: Reproducing 70B experiments requires suitable GPU
  capacity and some repository workflows require external model API keys.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** The release has not been

### EXT-146 — Limited-human best-arm auditing occupies the generic audit intervention

**Finding.** Ao et al. study fixed-confidence best-arm identification when a
biased LLM judge scores every sample and expensive human reference labels are
selectively audited. They propose inverse-propensity-weighted residual
correction, anytime-valid confidence sequences, and an adaptive algorithm that
concentrates audits on unreliable contexts and close arms. Their LUCB-style
rule stops when the leading arm's lower confidence bound exceeds every
competitor's upper confidence bound, and Section 6 reports synthetic repeated
simulation experiments. Therefore,
“use a small, targeted, design-corrected human audit to preserve model
selection” is not by itself an unoccupied methods contribution.

A distinct empirical contribution remains possible if it tests whether such
methods survive genuine proxy optimization, optimization-induced
distribution shift, an audit-aware model, held-out failure mechanisms, or a
prespecified safety-gating decision rather than ordinary stationary
best-arm identification.

**Status.** provisional at the cited preprint scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, not independently reproduced

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Ruicheng Ao, Hongyu Chen, Siyang Gao, Hanwei Li, and David
  Simchi-Levi, “Best Arm Identification with LLM Judges and Limited Human,”
  arXiv:2601.21471, Sections 3–6,
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21471>, submitted 2026-01-29, retrieved
  2026-07-24 and full text rechecked 2026-07-25.
- Method: Checked the primary full text for the problem definition,
  inverse-probability-weighted residual estimator, confidence sequences,
  adaptive-audit rule, LUCB-style stopping condition, theoretical claims, and
  synthetic experiments. The novelty implication is an inference from that
  stated scope relative to the proposed generic audit angle.
- Access limitations: Public preprint; no independent code execution or
  theorem verification was performed.
- Expanded audit and independent challenge:
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/primary-source-audit.md`
  and
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/review-source-audit.md`.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** The full paper and any released
code must be reproduced before asserting exact equivalence to a planned
implementation. Section 3 describes observing the current context before arm
choice, while the theorem filtration and Algorithm 1 appear to choose the arm
before the next context. If arm choice depends on context, the simple
within-arm proxy mean may not target the marginal-context arm mean without an
additional propensity correction or assumption. This scope question remains
unresolved. The reported synthetic experiments also do not establish
optimization-induced shift, strategic audit evasion, robot-domain validity,
or safety-gating outcomes. Those differences are candidate contribution
deltas, not validated gaps.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `provisional at the cited preprint scope` after
  checking the primary arXiv record. Full-paper and implementation comparison
  remain required before a final novelty claim.
- 2026-07-25 — Retained `provisional at the cited preprint scope` after
  full-text inspection verified the estimator, confidence-sequence,
  LUCB-style stopping, and synthetic-experiment descriptions, but an
  independent challenge identified unresolved context/arm timing ambiguity
  relevant to theorem scope. No theorem or code reproduction was performed.

### EXT-147 — Capability-gap oversight scaling is already a direct research program

**Finding.** Engels et al. explicitly model oversight success as a function
of overseer and overseen capability. They validate the framework on modified
Nim and apply it to four oversight games—Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, and
Wargames—using oversight- and deception-specific Elo parameters linked to a
general-capability proxy. Consequently, a new proposal cannot claim novelty
from merely crossing generator and evaluator capability levels and fitting a
failure surface.

A narrower contribution may remain in causal manipulation of proxy
optimization, independently measured capability constructs, decision regret,
audit-aware adaptation, or held-out prediction across model families and
failure mechanisms.

**Status.** provisional at the cited paper scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, not independently reproduced

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Joshua Engels, David D. Baek, Subhash Kantamneni, and Max Tegmark,
  “Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight,” arXiv:2504.18530,
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18530>, submitted 2025-04-25, abstract and
  linked manuscript, retrieved 2026-07-24.
- Method: Checked the primary arXiv record for the stated capability
  parameterization, validation game, four oversight games, and nested
  scalable-oversight analysis. The novelty implication is an inference
  relative to the proposed capability-boundary angle.
- Access limitations: Public paper; experiments and fitted scaling laws were
  not independently reproduced here.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** The paper's general capability
proxy, game abstractions, model set, and transport beyond the studied games
require full-method review before using it as a baseline. It does not
establish a universal capability boundary, and it does not necessarily test
the proposed audit intervention.

### EXT-148 — Decision-specific best-of-N judge failure is already demonstrated

**Finding.** Landesberg reports a 5,000-prompt best-of-four experiment using
Chatbot Arena data in which an LLM judge has global correlation \(0.471\),
within-instance correlation \(0.267\), recovers 21.0% of the oracle
improvement over random choice, and selects the top candidate with probability
31.6%. The 21.0% value is normalized recovery, not top-1 accuracy. The
preprint attributes the gap to weak within-prompt ranking signal and frequent
pointwise-score ties, and reports higher recovery from an explicit pairwise
judge in a matched best-of-two audit. Thus, showing that a judge with
acceptable global metrics performs poorly at best-of-\(N\) selection is not
by itself a new decision-validity result.

**Status.** provisional at the cited preprint scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, not independently reproduced

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Eddie Landesberg, “When LLM Judge Scores Look Good but Best-of-N

  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12520>, submitted 2026-03-12, Table 2,
  Tables 4–5, and Section 7.5, retrieved 2026-07-24 and rechecked 2026-07-25.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** This is a single-author recent

### EXT-149 — Generic evaluation tooling is commercially occupied

**Finding.** Current commercial AI-evaluation products already provide broad
combinations of automated evaluators, side-by-side experiments, benchmarking,
human-in-the-loop annotation, monitoring, and deployment or quality-gate
workflows. Braintrust documents systematic experiments, configuration
comparison, continuous production evaluation, and human review within release
workflows. Patronus documents automated evaluators, benchmarking, human
feedback, adversarial testing, and production monitoring. In robotics,
Lightwheel's RoboFinals page describes an industrial simulation-evaluation
platform for robot foundation models but, on 2026-07-25, also displays
“Coming soon” and “Book a Demo” while claiming partner/private use. NVIDIA's
RoboLab article describes statistical intervals and diagnostics but says key
features were planned for August 2026 productization. Isaac Lab-Arena is
documented as available open source, while natural-language authoring and
agentic/root-cause features are marked coming soon.

These product scopes make “an AI evaluation dashboard with targeted human
review” a crowded horizontal startup position. A distinguishable business
wedge would need to sell a higher-value decision outcome—such as
release/withhold, candidate selection, or abstention with quantified
decision-risk—or specialize where target evaluation is unusually expensive,
as in physical robot trials. NIST's AI RMF separately identifies documented,
repeatable test, evaluation, verification, and validation processes and
human-AI oversight roles, providing an institutional use case for
decision-assurance evidence without establishing private willingness to pay
for any particular product.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited product-page/date scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Braintrust, “Evaluate systematically,”
  <https://www.braintrust.dev/docs/evaluate>, product documentation retrieved
  2026-07-24.
- Source: Patronus AI product documentation,
  <https://docs.patronus.ai/docs> and
  <https://www.patronus.ai/products>, retrieved 2026-07-24.
- Source: Lightwheel, “RoboFinals,”
  <https://www.lightwheel.ai/robofinals>, product page retrieved 2026-07-24
  and rechecked 2026-07-25.
- Source: NVIDIA, “How to Evaluate General-Purpose Robot Policies for
  Real-World Deployment,”
  <https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/how-to-evaluate-general-purpose-robot-policies-for-real-world-deployment/>,
  retrieved 2026-07-25.
- Source: NVIDIA, “Isaac Lab-Arena,”
  <https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab-arena>, retrieved 2026-07-25.
- Source: NIST AI Risk Management Framework Core,
  <https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/>, Govern, Map,

  proposed generic evaluator-plus-human-audit product and checked NIST's

- Access limitations: Product pages describe vendor capabilities but do not

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** This is a bounded current-product
check, not a complete competitive landscape or proof of market demand.
The official pages support only page-and-date-bounded availability
descriptions; they do not establish a market-wide absence or independently
verify partner-use claims.
Customer urgency, budgets, procurement, integration cost, and willingness to
pay for decision assurance require discovery interviews and paid pilots. The
recommended wedge is a strategic inference, not an externally established
business outcome.

### EXT-158 — Sequential robot-policy comparison already supports continue, decide, and no-decision

**Finding.** STEP formulates pairwise robot-policy comparison as a sequential
binary decision with `Continue`, `AcceptNull`, or `RejectNull`, permits
additional IID Bernoulli trials to be appended within a prespecified maximum
budget, controls a prespecified Type-I error, and can terminate without a
decision when evidence remains inadequate. It reports real-hardware and
SimplerEnv examples and comparative rollout savings. Generic
`advance / test more / abstain` logic for robot-policy comparison is therefore
already occupied; this does not establish equivalence to a learned-evaluator
certificate.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited RSS 2025 paper scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Snyder et al., “Is Your Imitation Learning Policy Better than Mine?
  Policy Comparison with Near-Optimal Stopping,” RSS 2025, DOI
  `10.15607/RSS.2025.XXI.077`, Sections I–III, Assumption 1, Equations 2 and 4,
  Table I, and Section V-C,
  <https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss21/p077.html>, retrieved
  2026-07-25.
- Method: Inspected the primary paper for its sequential states, IID
  Bernoulli assumption, maximum budget, error-control claim, hardware and
  simulator examples, and stated rollout savings.
- Adjudicated audit and independent challenge:
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/primary-source-audit.md`
  and
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/review-source-audit.md`.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** STEP reduces multitask and
multipolicy cases to pairwise comparisons and uses binary outcomes. The
hardware examples do not provide independent latent truth labels for decision
error. It does not validate a learned world-model evaluator, top-k regret,
multi-metric deployment loss, or a general simulation-to-reality certificate.

### EXT-159 — Active robot evaluation already selects the next policy-task experiment

**Finding.** Anwar et al. formulate robot-policy evaluation as active
selection among policy-task experiment units using MC-dropout uncertainty and
expected information gain, including a cost-aware variant. Their experiments
show clearer improvements for estimating means than complete distributions;
expected information gain is not uniformly dominant across the evaluated
datasets. Best-average, ranking, and worst-task decisions are stated as future
directions. “Choose what to test next” is therefore not itself novel in robot
evaluation, while terminal error-controlled certification remains a distinct
question.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited CoRL 2025 paper scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Anwar et al., “Efficient Evaluation of Multi-Task Robot Policies
  With Active Experiment Selection,” CoRL 2025, Sections III–IV and VII–VIII,
  <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v305/anwar25a.html>, retrieved 2026-07-25.
- Method: Inspected the primary paper for target quantities, MC-dropout,
  expected-information-gain and cost-aware acquisition, empirical
  comparisons, and stated future directions.
- Adjudicated audit and independent challenge:
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/primary-source-audit.md`
  and
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/review-source-audit.md`.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** The study does not establish that
active allocation is ineffective outside its evaluated datasets and may
provide components for a future certificate. Its evaluated allocation
problem is not an independently validated terminal winner, regret, coverage,
or abstention decision.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-25 — Created as `confirmed at the cited CoRL 2025 paper scope` after
  primary full-text inspection and an independent evidence-path challenge.

### EXT-160 — Bayesian best-arm identification already includes an abstention budget

**Finding.** Huang, Hou, and Tan formulate Bayesian fixed-budget best-arm
identification with a global prior-average abstention budget \(\alpha\). Their
method allocates abstention to ambiguous problem instances and analyzes
undetected error asymptotically. Generic novelty for adding abstention to
best-arm selection is therefore occupied at the preprint's stated scope;
per-instance frequentist coverage and robot-domain empirical validity are not
established.

**Status.** provisional at the cited preprint scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, not independently reproduced

**Evidence and trace.**

- Source: Huang, Hou, and Tan, “Bayesian Best-Arm Identification with
  Abstention,” arXiv:2606.29203v1, DOI `10.48550/arXiv.2606.29203`,
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29203>, retrieved 2026-07-25.
- Method: Inspected the primary arXiv record and manuscript for the
  fixed-budget Bayesian formulation, global abstention budget,
  ambiguous-instance allocation, and asymptotic claims.
- Adjudicated audit and independent challenge:
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/primary-source-audit.md`
  and
  `ppi-gold-bias/research/decision-assurance-collision-audit/review-source-audit.md`.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** This is a recent preprint in a
bandit theory/simulation setting. The audit did not reproduce its theorems or
identify robot-domain empirical validation. Its Bayesian global
prior-average abstention constraint is not the same as per-instance
frequentist coverage.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-25 — Created as `provisional at the cited preprint scope` after
  primary-source inspection and independent challenge; theorem reproduction
  and robot-domain validation remain open.

### EXT-140 — DROID records timing information that the audited RoboArena MP4/NPZ interface does not preserve

**Finding.** At DROID platform commit
`33ae6a67274f36d2e29525b86f23a56616ef43a7`, trajectory collection starts
ZED SVO recording before the control loop. Each loop reads the robot state and
cameras into one observation with separate timestamp dictionaries, obtains the
policy/controller action, steps the robot, then writes the observation and
action as one timestep. The camera wrapper randomizes multi-camera read order
and records camera-specific read timestamps.

The pinned RoboArena release audited in EXT-137 exposes converted MP4 videos
and NPZ state/action arrays, not the original SVO plus per-frame camera
timestamp stream. A decoded census found that all 114 400-state records have
401 video frames, while the single 132-state record has 132 frames. This
complete and consistent count pattern still does
not by itself determine whether the correct alignment is frame 0 with state 0,
frame 1 with state 0, a timestamp-nearest rule, or another conversion rule.
The acquisition source narrows the required validation artifact to raw
timestamps or an independent motion alignment oracle; it does not identify an
offset from release lengths.

**Status.** confirmed at the cited DROID commit and audited RoboArena-release
scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified and locally code-path inspected

**Evidence and trace.**

- DROID platform,
  <https://github.com/droid-dataset/droid/tree/33ae6a67274f36d2e29525b86f23a56616ef43a7>,
  `droid/trajectory_utils/misc.py`, `droid/robot_env.py`,
  `droid/camera_utils/wrappers/multi_camera_wrapper.py`, and
  `droid/camera_utils/camera_readers/zed_camera.py`, retrieved and inspected
  2026-07-24.
- Local immutable checkout:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/work/external/droid-platform`, commit
  `33ae6a67274f36d2e29525b86f23a56616ef43a7`. The inspected collection path
  begins SVO recording before the loop, calls `env.get_observation()` before
  action selection and `env.step()`, and writes the joined timestep after the
  step. `RobotEnv.get_observation()` retains robot-state and camera timestamp
  dictionaries.
- RoboArena release schema and sampled length evidence:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/oscar-input-reconstruction/result-historical-input-contract.json`
  and EXT-137.

**Uncertainty and remaining validation.** The public source describes the
DROID acquisition path, not necessarily every site-specific RoboArena
conversion revision. The exact MP4/NPZ export code and raw timestamps for the
sampled release records were not located. Offset selection still requires
timestamped raw episodes or independent keypoint/mask alignment on development
and untouched holdout sessions.

**Status history.**

- 2026-07-24 — Created as `confirmed at the cited DROID commit and audited
  RoboArena-release scope` after checking the acquisition call order,
  timestamp fields, SVO recording boundary, and the already pinned RoboArena

- 2026-07-24 — Evidence updated without changing status after a decoded-frame
  census replaced the earlier sampled length evidence: all 115 matched
  records now support the stated N/N+1 pattern, but no released timestamp or
  exporter-index oracle identifies the semantic offset.

### EXT-143 — Pinned OSCAR inference executes on an A40 after undeclared repairs, but exact same-seed decoded output does not repeat

**Finding.** OSCAR public source commit
`4dea2f657e221b0ff24c895fcc8ab4d46d5a9adb` and OSCAR-2B revision
`c9781ffa7dd8556d862d7d9f338a2ea008a58ca6` executed successfully on one
secure-cloud NVIDIA A40 after environment-only repair. All three generated
H.264 outputs fully decoded to 81 RGB frames at 640×480. The five-step case
used 31,263 MiB peak GPU memory and 113.86 seconds wall time; two 35-step cases
used 36,719/37,459 MiB and 247.48/244.24 seconds.

The frozen full-smoke rule failed because identical `droid_TRI` inputs with
seed 44, 35 steps, and guidance 6.0 produced different encoded files and
different decoded-RGB hashes:
`a87e72e2a371cfbe3d4f02e85528e114efaed9c9543c8475de2418bd6aeb24bc`
versus
`b1e0aeea642f895b55da5da52ee452ad83cdd27bf2f64fab55b64395c6908025`.
A subsequent decoded-pixel audit found 0/81 exactly equal frames, 57,853,816
of 74,649,600 unequal RGB channel values (77.50%), global MAE 5.228 uint8
levels, RMSE 18.259, pairwise PSNR 22.901 dB, and maximum absolute difference
243. Frame-0 MAE was 0.990 and frame-80 MAE was 12.504. Thus A40
executability/media integrity passed, while exact cross-process decoded-output
repeatability did not.

The five-step encoded SHA-256 was
`2243fb85c8cecf9839c35b4db1fda78bae077fafe450d06407298b1b1c491cf1`,
not the README's `e9bd9430d9828f4d` prefix. The earlier audit interpreted the
README prefix as an encoded-output oracle. That interpretation is
superseded: the README does not define whether it hashes encoded MP4, decoded
RGB, or wrapper-returned uint8 frames, and it does not state whether the
QA-only `rgb_video` input was supplied. The wrappers do not encode MP4, while
the completed five-step run used QA RGB and compared encoded MP4 bytes.
Accordingly, the arithmetic mismatch is retained but cannot adjudicate the
repository's cross-surface parity claim.

The public dependency contract was not self-sufficient at the pinned commit.
The README described Transformer Engine as optional and said public cases used
the SDPA fallback; the imported inference graph hard-required
`transformer_engine`, while `requirements_minimal.txt` separately said TE
2.11 was required but did not install it. After a pinned TE 2.11 source build,
the graph next hard-imported `pytest`, also omitted from the minimal
requirements. No OSCAR source file was edited. The successful environment used
TE commit `c188b533cc3721ca9c6bbfd26148f5cf60108c25`,
`pytest==9.1.1`, Python 3.11.13, PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128, and auxiliary
Cosmos-Reason1 revision
`3210bec0495fdc7a8d3dbb8d58da5711eab4b423`.

The deeper source audit identified a concrete determinism-control defect.
`inference._core.setup_backends()` first sets cuDNN deterministic `True` and
benchmark `False`; the subsequently called `load_model_from_checkpoint()`
overwrites those values from `config.trainer.cudnn`. The inherited released
defaults are deterministic `False` and benchmark `True`, and the OSCAR
experiment does not override them. The loader also enables TF32, while the
inference path does not enable PyTorch deterministic-algorithm enforcement or
a deterministic cuBLAS workspace. This proves that the apparent setup flags
were not the effective inference flags. It is a plausible causal mechanism,
not yet a causal result, because no intermediate tensors or one-factor
post-load-flag rerun were retained.

Authorized layerwise attempt 07 did not reach checkpoint loading because its
launcher omitted the one-rank `torchrun` rendezvous. It was not retried. The
repaired launcher then executed in attempt 08 from a fresh, fully gated A40
runtime. Baseline repeat A loaded the pinned model and produced an 81-frame
output, but the old trace-completeness contract expected five scheduler
updates, ten denoiser calls, and 80 denoiser-condition tensor rows; execution
produced six, twelve, and 96. The runner exited 1 before writing the detailed
trace. Baseline B and all intervention arms did not start, and no retry
occurred.

The attempt-08 mismatch is resolved as a harness/protocol error, not upstream
drift or a scientific nondeterminism result. The pinned experiment sets
`use_kerras_sigma_at_inference=True`. The pinned scheduler's Karras branch
constructs `num_inference_steps + 1` sigma points, converts every point to a
timestep, and the model loops over all timesteps. Requested `num_steps=5`
therefore executes six updates. Classifier-free guidance calls the denoiser
twice per update, producing twelve calls. The earlier nominal-five-step public
smoke already displayed six progress iterations, so this behavior predated
the diagnostic harness. The evidence does not identify whether the authors
intended the \(N+1\) interface semantics.

Attempt 08 establishes only fixed-environment execution feasibility, one
structurally valid output, the observed 6/12/96 counts, and bounded operational
accounting. It does not adjudicate same-seed repeatability, the first divergent
internal tensor, or any intervention effect. The corrected next-run contract
keeps requested `num_steps=5`, freezes the six integer timesteps
`[995, 984, 941, 742, 228, 9]`, expects twelve denoiser calls and 96 condition
rows, probes the exact scheduler on CPU before model loading, and preserves a
partial trace before a future completeness error.

**Status.** confirmed for the pinned A40 environment; public hash
unadjudicated and first divergent internal tensor/cause unresolved

**Evidence basis.** source-verified and independently executed with full
decode and immutable evidence archive

### EXT-151 — No available source immediately supplies the target-valid prospective automated-rater control cohort

**Finding.** The held-out automated-rater design requires 52 new positive and
52 new negative unique source sessions after its
2026-07-24T23:34:51Z freeze. Four predeclared task families with 13 positive
and 13 negative sources each guarantee that the frozen development split can
remove eight records per class while every family remains represented in the
88-source validation cohort and no family can exceed half of that cohort.
This is a deterministic split-coverage calculation, not a population-sampling
or power claim.

No current public or repository-local source supplies that target-valid
cohort. The current RoboArena dump contributes zero sessions after the
prospective intake, and derivatives of the 441-video historical OSCAR release
remain the same exposed source sessions. The preferred route is purpose-built
private post-freeze DROID/Franka collection, converted through the exact
intended OSCAR presentation path and independently truth-reviewed at the
presented-video level.

The official DROID simulation fallback is not truth-ready at its inspected
commit. It exposes exactly three instructions—cube into bowl, can into mug,
and banana into bin—which are all instances of one container-placement
family. Its environment defines an empty reward configuration and only a
timeout termination. It can be extended into a reproducible acquisition
substrate, but doing so requires at least four distinct task families,
explicit state predicates, tested positive and negative trajectories, and
retained simulator traces.

Deterministic skeleton/composited controls and general simulation frameworks
can validate decoding, packaging, instruction swaps, duplicates, response
parsing, and fail-closed behavior on their own finite cohorts. They do not by
themselves establish task-success perception on OSCAR-generated robot videos.
Simulator-state success also does not prove that a transformed OSCAR output
visibly satisfies the task; the exact output requires independent truth
review.

**Status.** confirmed at the pinned source/current-release scope

**Evidence basis.** source-verified, reproduced source audit, derived

**Evidence and trace.**

- Canonical feasibility review, source locations, split-coverage derivation,
  route ranking, and acquisition contract:
  `sim2real-correlation-audit/research/prospective-agent-rater-validation/review-control-acquisition-feasibility.md`.
- DROID collection repository, pinned local commit
  `33ae6a67274f36d2e29525b86f23a56616ef43a7`, especially
  `droid/user_interface/data_collector.py`,
  `droid/user_interface/gui.py`, and `docs/the-droid-dataset.md`. The source
  retains operator success/failure state and multi-camera recordings; these
  are source-truth inputs, not automatic truth for a later generated video.
- DROID simulation repository,
  <https://github.com/arhanjain/sim-evals>, cleanly cloned and inspected at
  commit `3a6b0e8177f696947f49c082728f10ef5133ede1`, especially `run_eval.py` and
